title: Bridges and tests: callbackFlow, Reactor and runTest
goal: By the end you can wrap a listener API in callbackFlow without leaking the listener or losing values, predict how Reactor demand and Flow suspension map onto each other, give Java callers a Flux, and test flows on virtual time knowing what runCurrent, advanceTimeBy, advanceUntilIdle and Turbine show and hide.
opening:
The old wireless oven probe from the coroutines track is still in the kitchen drawer. You push it into the roast, and it calls you. Its library has a **listener**: you register a function, and the probe calls it on its own thread (a worker that runs code) with every new reading, until you unregister it. Next door, the neighbour's kitchen runs on Reactor, a line of stations where each one asks the one before it for a number of items at a time. And before a big dinner, the house holds a rehearsal on a fake clock.

A flow fits none of these. It waits to be collected, it hands values over by suspending, and its delays take real time. The easy trap is to wrap the probe in a few lines that work in a demo, and then lose readings, or leave the listener behind, in the first busy hour.

Hot flows in depth shared values inside one program. In this lesson, we'll bridge the probe with `callbackFlow`, survive the burst it sends on connect, cross into Reactor and back, and rehearse it all on virtual time. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A test runs `backgroundScope.launch { probe.readings().collect { got += it } }`, where `readings()` is a correct `callbackFlow` that registers a listener, and on the very next line calls `probe.fire(reading)`. Then it calls `runCurrent()`. What is in `got`?
options: Nothing: the listener wasn't registered when the reading fired
warmup.why: On the default `StandardTestDispatcher`, `launch` only queues the collector. The `callbackFlow` block that calls `register` runs in a producer coroutine when the scheduler next runs, which is at `runCurrent()`, after the fire. The reading found no listener and went nowhere. Real code has the same gap.

sections.h: A burst of 200 on connect: 64 spots and one waiting hand
sections.body:
The probe keeps its readings while nobody listens, and on connect it replays them in one burst, from its own thread, one callback after another. Fire 200 readings into a default `callbackFlow` while its collector waits in `receive()`, and 135 `trySend` calls fail. The other 65 got through: 64 onto the shelf (`Channel.BUFFERED`), and one handed straight to the receiver that was already waiting, before the shelf was touched. So a shelf of 64 takes 65 when someone is waiting at the hatch. Better to know that before a test counts it for you.

`trySend` returns a `ChannelResult` that says whether it worked. Ignore it, and the 135 failures are silent losses. After the channel is closed it fails too, with `isClosed=true`. The fix is a policy you choose on purpose. A `buffer(...)` or `conflate()` right after `callbackFlow { }` fuses into its one channel (the shelves snapping together from Buffering), so it changes that channel instead of adding a second one:

| After `callbackFlow { }` | `trySend` failures | The collector got |
|---|---|---|
| nothing (64, `SUSPEND`) | 135 | 65 accepted |
| `.buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED)` | 0 | all 200 |
| `.conflate()` | 0 | `[0, 199]`: the first went to the waiting receiver, the last stayed in the one spot |
| `.buffer(10, DROP_OLDEST)` | 0 | `[0, 190, 191, ..., 199]` |

```kotlin
fun FakeProbe.readings(): Flow<ProbeReading> = callbackFlow { /* register, trySend, awaitClose */ }
    .buffer(500)   // fused: the bridge's own channel now holds the 500 stored readings
```

```java
// Java equivalent: Flux.create buffers without limit by default (OverflowStrategy.BUFFER);
// onBackpressureBuffer(500) caps it and fails with an overflow error past 500
Flux<ProbeReading> readings = Flux.create(sink -> { /* register, sink.next, onDispose */ })
    .onBackpressureBuffer(500);
```

`trySendBlocking(e)` looks like the safe version. It is `trySend` with a fallback of `runBlocking { send(e) }`, so when the shelf is full it blocks the probe's own thread until there is room. With the probe's thread pushing 200 readings and a collector that takes 2 ms each, `trySend` let the thread finish in about 1 ms and lost 135, while `trySendBlocking` lost none and held the probe's thread for about 340 ms. (That run uses the real clock, so your numbers will differ.) Use it only when the library runs your callback on a worker thread of its own, and making that thread wait is how you slow it down. Pick `UNLIMITED` only when the producer is known to stop. For a feed where only the latest value matters, `conflate()` drops readings in a way you can explain.

**A failed trySend is a lost reading. Size the shelf for the burst, or choose what to drop.**

Check yourself: what does the collector get from the same burst after `.buffer(10, DROP_LATEST)`? The probe now feeds a flow without losing anything. The neighbour wants the readings too, and her kitchen speaks Reactor.

sections.h: Across the Reactor bridge, demand becomes suspension
sections.body:
Reactor follows **Reactive Streams**, a small standard set of Java interfaces for streams, and it makes the subscriber say how much it can take, with `request(n)`. That number is called **demand**. A Flow has no such call: it suspends. The bridges in the kotlinx-coroutines-reactive and kotlinx-coroutines-reactor modules translate one into the other.

`Publisher.asFlow()` works like a diner with an order pad, sitting at the end of the neighbour's line of stations. It orders 64, eats them, and orders 64 more after every 64 it has passed on. (A `Flux` is a `Publisher`, so `flux.asFlow()` is this same function.) The items wait in a channel of that size, and `buffer` sets the size of the order:

| Flow side | Requests sent to a 300-item `Flux` |
|---|---|
| `asFlow()` | 64 after 0, 64, 128, 192 and 256 |
| `asFlow().buffer(10)` | 10 every 10 |
| `asFlow().buffer(0)` | 1 every 1 |
| `asFlow().conflate()` or `.buffer(UNLIMITED)` | `Long.MAX_VALUE`, once |
| `asFlow().take(3)` | 64, then cancel: the 61 extra already in the channel are thrown away |

That is a refill in batches. Reactor's own operators top up earlier: `publishOn` asked a Flow-backed Flux for 256 and then 192 at a time, and `limitRate(10)` for 10 and then 8.

`Flow.asFlux()` and `asPublisher()` go the other way. Nothing runs until the first `request(n)`. Then each `emit` calls `onNext` right there, inside `emit`, and counts the demand down. When it reaches 0, the flow suspends inside that `emit`, and a later `request` resumes it. After `request(2)` the subscriber had `[1, 2]`, and `emit` had returned only for 1: the flow was parked inside `emit(2)`. Cancelling the subscription cancels the flow's coroutine, so a `callbackFlow` underneath runs its `awaitClose`.

Two details bite in real programs. The bridge runs the flow on `Dispatchers.Unconfined` unless you pass a dispatcher (the part that picks the thread a coroutine runs on), so the flow and every Reactor operator after it run on whichever thread resumed it: the subscriber's thread at first, `kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor` after a `delay`, and the probe's own thread under a probe bridge. Pass `asFlux(dispatcher)`, or add `publishOn` before anything slow downstream. And Reactor's `Context`, a small map of values that travels with a subscription, crosses in both directions. Through `asFlux()`, a table number written with `contextWrite` was visible inside the flow as a `ReactorContext` element. The other way, a `ReactorContext` in the coroutine reaches a publisher collected with `asFlow()` only when kotlinx-coroutines-reactor is on the classpath, the list of libraries the program can see, because that module supplies the piece that injects it, found with `ServiceLoader`.

Java can't call `Flow.collect`, which it sees as `Object collect(FlowCollector, Continuation)`. Give Java a face built in Kotlin:

```kotlin
class ProbeApi(private val probe: FakeProbe) {
    fun readings(): Flow<ProbeReading> = probe.readings()          // for Kotlin callers
    fun readingsFlux(): Flux<ProbeReading> = readings().asFlux()   // for Java and Reactor callers
}
```

```java
// Java caller: only Reactor types, no Flow and no Continuation
List<ProbeReading> firstTwo = new ProbeApi(probe).readingsFlux().take(2).collectList().block();
```

For a single result, a `CompletableFuture` built with `scope.future { }` is the better face, as lesson 11 of the coroutines track showed.

**Give Java a Flux or a future, never a Flow.**

Check yourself: how many requests does `asFlow().buffer(10)` send to a 300-item `Flux`, and why one more than 30? Every bridge in this lesson has a timing story, and testing timing on a real clock is slow and flaky. So the house rehearses.

sections.h: Turbine writes down every value, and that is its blind spot
sections.body:
**Turbine** 1.2.1 (`app.cash.turbine`, a test dependency of this lab module) is a test library that turns a flow into a list of events you read one by one:

```kotlin
probe.readings().test {          // collects before the block runs: the listener is registered
    probe.fire(first)
    assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo(first)
    probe.fail(IOException("probe connection lost"))
    assertThat(awaitError()).hasMessage("probe connection lost")
}
```

```java
// Java equivalent: StepVerifier subscribes, then runs each step in order
StepVerifier.create(api.readingsFlux())
    .then(() -> probe.fire(first))
    .expectNext(first)
    .then(() -> probe.fail(new IOException("probe connection lost")))
    .expectErrorMessage("probe connection lost")
    .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(5));
```

Picture the rehearsal's note-taker. `test { }` runs the flow up to its first suspension before your block starts, so a SharedFlow is subscribed and a `callbackFlow` listener is registered by then, which removes the race from the first section. Every event goes into her notebook, an unlimited channel, in order. You read it with `awaitItem()`, `awaitComplete()` and `awaitError()`, which hands you the error as an event instead of throwing it. An event you never read fails the test with `Unconsumed events found`, unless you end with `cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()`. If no new event arrives within 3 s of real time, the test fails with `No value produced in 3s`. The flow's own `delay` calls stay virtual inside `runTest`; only Turbine's wait is real. To follow two flows at once, call `testIn(backgroundScope)` inside `turbineScope { }`. Outside it, `testIn` compiles and then fails at run time with `Turbine can only collect flows within a TurbineContext`.

The note-taker hears everything, and that is her blind spot. Turbine collects on `UnconfinedTestDispatcher`, so it takes each value the instant it is sent. It saw COOKING, which the Standard collector of the last section never got. It also took all 500 readings of a burst through a 64-spot `callbackFlow`, where a Standard collector got 65. She never misses a word, which makes her a poor witness to what a slower listener would miss.

So use Turbine to check what a flow emits and in what order. Don't use it to test skipped values, buffer sizes or a slow collector. For those, collect with a Standard collector in `backgroundScope` and drive the clock yourself, as the lab's burst test does. And on a SharedFlow with no replay, a value emitted before `test { }` starts is gone, so the test fails with `No value produced`.

**Turbine shows what a flow says, not what a slow listener hears. Test buffers with a Standard collector.**

Check yourself: which test in the lab would still pass with a 64-spot buffer if you rewrote it with Turbine, and why? Every bridge in this lesson sits on top of something that waits: a probe's thread, a Reactor line, a clock. Underneath them all is the place where waiting really happens.

compare.title: A probe bridge: Flux.create next to callbackFlow

java.title: ProbeReadings.java (Reactor)

kotlin.title: ProbeReadings.kt (callbackFlow)

compare.note: The shapes match line for line, and four things differ. Registration time: `Flux.create` registers inside `subscribe()`, while `callbackFlow` registers when its producer coroutine first runs, so a reading fired right after `collect` starts can be lost. Cleanup: `callbackFlow` throws when its block returns without `awaitClose`, and Reactor lets a missing `onDispose` leak the listener with no message. Buffering: Kotlin's channel holds 64 (65 with a waiting receiver) and makes you look at `trySend`'s result; Reactor buffers without limit unless you add a policy. Threads: `sink.next` calls the subscriber's `onNext` on the probe's thread, while the Kotlin collector runs on its own dispatcher and the probe's thread only drops the reading into the channel. That holds until you turn the flow into a Flux with plain `asFlux()`, whose `Unconfined` default puts the subscriber back on the probe's thread.

hints: `close(error)` and `close()` belong to the `ProducerScope` the block runs in, so you can call them from inside the listener object.

`Expected size: 500 but was: 65` is the default 64 spots plus the one reading handed to the waiting collector. A `buffer(...)` right after `callbackFlow { }` is fused into its channel. `Channel.UNLIMITED` passes too; a number states how much memory you allow.
Don't reach for `trySendBlocking`. In the burst test the probe's thread is the test's only thread, the one the collector needs in order to run.
`asFlux()` is in `kotlinx.coroutines.reactor`. It starts the flow at the first `request(n)` and cancels it when the subscription is cancelled, which is what the Java tests check.

drill.title: A listener bridge, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. A made-up kitchen scale library has `fun subscribe(onWeight: (Weight) -> Unit, onFailure: (Throwable) -> Unit): Cancellable`. Write `fun KitchenScale.weights(): Flow<Weight>` that never blocks the scale's thread, fails the flow on `onFailure`, holds a burst of 1,000 weights, and cancels the subscription whatever ends the collection. Then say in a comment what happens if you leave out the cleanup line.

alt.title: Java equivalent

recap: `callbackFlow` registers when its producer coroutine first runs, after `collect` starts, so a value fired in between is lost. Tests wait for the registration; Turbine's `test { }` does it for you. Reactor's `Flux.create` registers inside `subscribe()`.

`awaitClose { unregister() }` runs on `take(n)`, cancellation, `close(error)` and `close()`. Without it, collecting throws the exact `IllegalStateException` shown in the lesson. Use `channelFlow` for your own coroutines and `suspendCancellableCoroutine` for a callback that fires once.

The bridge holds 64 by default plus one handed to a waiting receiver, so 65 of a 200-reading burst got in. Check `trySend`'s result, and choose a fused `buffer(n)`, `conflate()` or `UNLIMITED` (for a producer known to stop) on purpose. `trySendBlocking` blocks the library's thread.

`Publisher.asFlow()` requests 64, then 64 more after each 64; `buffer(n)` makes it `request(n)`. `asFlux()` starts at the first request, calls `onNext` inside `emit` and suspends there when demand runs out, on `Unconfined` unless you pass a dispatcher. Give Java a `Flux` or a `CompletableFuture`, never a `Flow`.

`advanceTimeBy(n)` runs what is due before `now + n`, `runCurrent()` what is due now, and `advanceUntilIdle()` stops when only `backgroundScope` work is left. Turbine reads a flow in order with a 3 s real-time timeout, but it collects on `UnconfinedTestDispatcher`, so test skipped values and buffer sizes with a Standard collector.
The limit: these bridges and tests live inside one program, on top of threads and sockets that do the real waiting. How that waiting scales is the next track's subject.
closing:
We started with an old probe that calls you, a neighbour who speaks Reactor, and a rehearsal on a fake clock. `callbackFlow` fits a hatch to the probe: `trySend` fills a shelf sized for the burst, and `awaitClose` takes the listener down. `asFlow` and `asFlux` turn `request(n)` into suspension and back, and `runTest` and Turbine rehearse it all.

Now search your own code for `callbackFlow`, and check two lines in each: the `awaitClose`, and what happens to a failed `trySend`.

That ends the Flow track. Next, we'll go underneath, to the sockets where all this waiting happens. Why does a server with one thread per client run out of threads long before it runs out of work?

quiz.q: A `callbackFlow` with the default buffer is followed by `.conflate()`. Its collector is suspended, waiting for the first value, when the probe fires readings 0 to 199 one after another on its own thread. What does the collector get?
options: `[0, 199]`: the first went straight to the waiting collector, the last stayed in the one spot
quiz.why: `conflate()` is fused into the callbackFlow's channel and turns it into one spot that a new value overwrites. Reading 0 was handed directly to the receiver that was already waiting, so it never touched the spot; the spot then ended up holding 199. Lesson 4's `conflate()` works the same way.

quiz.q: A test runs `backgroundScope.launch { probe.readings().collect { got += it } }`, then `probe.fire(r)` on the next line, then `runCurrent()`. `readings()` is a correct `callbackFlow` with `awaitClose`. What are `got` and the listener count afterwards?
options: `[]` and 1: the listener registered after the fire
quiz.why: The default `StandardTestDispatcher` only queues the collector. Its producer coroutine, which calls `register`, runs at `runCurrent()`, after the fire, so the reading found no listener; from then on one listener is registered. Call `runCurrent()` before firing, or use Turbine's `test { }`.

quiz.q: Reactor code subscribes to `plates.asFlux()`, where `plates = flow { for (i in 1..10) { emit(i); log += i } }`, with a subscriber that calls `request(2)` and nothing more. What has the subscriber received, and what is in `log`?
options: Nothing yet: the flow waits for `request(64)`
`[1, 2]` and `[1]`: the flow is suspended inside `emit(2)`
quiz.why: `asFlux()` calls `onNext` inside `emit` and then counts the demand down. After the second `onNext` the demand is 0, so the flow suspends inside `emit(2)` before `log += 2` runs. A later `request(n)` resumes it. The 64 is the other direction: `Publisher.asFlow()` requests 64 at a time.

quiz.q: `cookAndServe()` sets a StateFlow to COOKING and then SERVED with no suspension between. Which test setup can show that a collector misses COOKING?
options: `backgroundScope.launch { status.toList(seen) }` on the default dispatcher, with `runCurrent()` before and after
quiz.why: Only a Standard collector waits for its turn, so it wakes to SERVED and records `[ORDERED, SERVED]`. Turbine and the Unconfined collector run inside each set and see all three. `take(3)` waits for a third value that never comes and fails with `UncompletedCoroutinesError`.

quiz.q: From lesson 7 of this track: people glance at `board.value`, where `board = readings.stateIn(houseScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null)`, and nobody ever collects it. What do they read?
options: `null` for ever: reading `.value` is not a subscription, so the feed never starts
The first reading, and never an update
quiz.why: `WhileSubscribed` starts the upstream from `subscriptionCount`, and `.value` doesn't count as a subscriber. Nothing ever starts the feed. A value that is only read through `.value` needs `Eagerly` or the suspend `stateIn(scope)`.

flashcards.front: When does a `callbackFlow` register its listener?
flashcards.back: When its producer coroutine first runs, after collection starts. A value fired before that is lost. Reactor's `Flux.create` registers inside `subscribe()`.

flashcards.front: What happens when a `callbackFlow` block returns without `awaitClose`?
flashcards.back: Collecting throws `IllegalStateException: 'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used in the end of callbackFlow block.`

flashcards.front: A collector waits on a default `callbackFlow`, and the probe fires 200 readings one after another. How many `trySend` calls succeed?
flashcards.back: 65: 64 buffered, plus 1 handed straight to the waiting receiver. The other 135 fail, and are lost unless you check the result.

flashcards.front: How does `Publisher.asFlow()` request from the publisher?
flashcards.back: `request(64)`, then 64 more after every 64 collected. `buffer(n)` makes it `request(n)`; `conflate()` and `UNLIMITED` request `Long.MAX_VALUE`.

flashcards.front: With `asFlux()`, where does the flow suspend when the subscriber's demand runs out?
flashcards.back: Inside `emit`, right after the `onNext` that used the last of the demand. A later `request(n)` resumes it.

flashcards.front: Tasks are due at +100 and +200 ms. What does `advanceTimeBy(100)` run?
flashcards.back: Nothing: it runs tasks due before now + 100 and leaves the clock at 100. `runCurrent()` then runs the task at 100.

flashcards.front: Why can't a Turbine test show a StateFlow skipping a value, or a buffer that is too small?
flashcards.back: Turbine collects on `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` and takes every value the instant it is sent, so it sees all values and the buffer never fills.

terms.plain: A flow builder for listener APIs. Its block registers a listener that sends into a channel, and `awaitClose` removes the listener when the flow ends.
Suspends the `callbackFlow` block until its channel is closed, then runs your cleanup, whatever ended the flow.
In Reactive Streams, the number of items a subscriber has asked for with `request(n)` and not yet received.
A `buffer`, `conflate` or `flowOn` placed right after a channel-based flow changes that flow's own channel instead of adding a second one.
The test scheduler's clock in `runTest`. It jumps to the next due task, so a `delay` takes no real time.
A scope inside `runTest` for coroutines that never end. They are cancelled when the test body ends, and `advanceUntilIdle()` doesn't wait for them.
A test library (`app.cash.turbine`) that collects a flow into a queue you read with `awaitItem`, `awaitComplete` and `awaitError`.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a friend why `probe.fire(r)` right after `backgroundScope.launch { probe.readings().collect { ... } }` loses the reading in a test, why rewriting the test with Turbine fixes that, and why Turbine would then hide a buffer that is too small.
explain_back.answer: On the default StandardTestDispatcher, launch only queues the collector. The callbackFlow's producer coroutine, which calls register, runs the next time the scheduler runs, so the fire happens with no listener and the reading goes nowhere. Turbine's test { } runs the flow up to its first suspension before the block starts, so by then the listener is registered. But Turbine collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher. Each trySend wakes it at once and the reading leaves the channel right away, so the channel never fills, and a 64-spot buffer passes a 500-reading burst. To test the buffer, collect with a Standard collector that can't run during the burst: launch it, call runCurrent() so it registers, fire the burst, call runCurrent() again and count.

deeper.body:
The JDK has its own Reactive Streams interfaces, `java.util.concurrent.Flow`, with `Publisher`, `Subscriber` and `Subscription`. kotlinx.coroutines bridges them in a separate artifact, `org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-jdk9:1.11.0`. It is a thin wrapper over the reactive module: `asFlow()`, `asPublisher()` and `collect` for the JDK types, with the same demand mapping (a JDK publisher over 150 items saw `request(64)` three times). You don't need the extra artifact. reactive-streams 1.0.4, already on this lab's classpath through kotlinx-coroutines-reactive, has `org.reactivestreams.FlowAdapters`, and `FlowAdapters.toPublisher(jdkPublisher).asFlow()` does the same job.

The JDK `HttpClient` shows why that matters. `client.sendAsync(request, BodyHandlers.ofPublisher())` is two bridges in one call. The `CompletableFuture` completes once, when the headers arrive, so it belongs to `await()`. The body is a JDK `Flow.Publisher<List<ByteBuffer>>` that delivers chunks as they come off the socket, so it belongs to `asFlow()`. In one run against a local server that wrote five lines 50 ms apart, the chunks arrived about 50 ms apart too. Wrapping the future in `callbackFlow` would be the wrong tool: a single result is a `suspendCancellableCoroutine` or `await()` job.

A few facts about the Reactor modules themselves. The README of kotlinx-coroutines-reactive calls `asPublisher` TCK-compliant, meaning it passes the official Reactive Streams compatibility tests. The subscription it creates has no parent job, so its lifetime belongs to the subscription and not to any scope. Element types must be non-null (`T : Any`), because Reactive Streams forbids `null` items. And the 1.11.0 reactor module declares reactor-core 3.4.1 in its pom; this course pins 3.8.8, and Gradle picks the higher version.
